query: High-entropy alloys are valued for combining strength and ductility. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their dynamic mechanical behavior, and what controlled comparison would reveal it? State the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the dynamic mechanical performance under high strain-rate (ballistic) conditions is governed primarily by rapid dislocation generation and multiplication. Alloys with stronger atomic bonding (i.e., lacking elements such as Mn that promote dislocation tangling) will produce higher dislocation densities and more effective strain hardening, thereby exhibiting superior resistance to dynamic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Two comparable HEAs, one with Mn (CrMnFeCoNi) and one without Mn (CrFeCoNi), prepared under similar processing conditions to ensure analogous grain size and microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Subject both alloys to high strain-rate deformation (e.g., ballistic impact tests or equivalent high strain-rate mechanical testing) with a control comparison at quasi-static strain rates.
generation.conditions: High strain rates (spanning the dynamic regime encountered under ballistic impact, e.g., from 10^0 s⁻¹ upward) under controlled temperature conditions (e.g., room temperature and/or cryogenic conditions) to minimize thermal effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of dislocations within the microstructure observed via techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or in situ diffraction methods.
generation.mechanism: Under the extreme strain rates, dislocation sources are activated more rapidly. In the Mn-free HEA, stronger atomic bonding facilitates a more uniform and increased dislocation multiplication and distribution, enhancing strain hardening mechanisms. By contrast, the presence of Mn leads to easier dislocation tangling and localized shear, which diminishes the beneficial strain hardening effect and reduces ballistic resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quasi-static baseline, the Mn-free CrFeCoNi alloy, when deformed at high strain rates, will demonstrate higher dislocation densities and an increased strain hardening rate compared to the Mn-containing CrMnFeCoNi alloy; these microstructural features correlate with enhanced dynamic mechanical performance and ballistic resistance.
generation.baseline: Both alloys under slow or quasi-static strain-rate deformation, where dislocation density differences are minimal and strain hardening is less pronounced.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in the dynamic (high strain-rate) deformation regime where dislocation kinetics dominate the mechanical response. It may be less applicable in conditions where other deformation mechanisms (such as extensive nano-twinning at cryogenic temperatures or very low strain-rate deformation) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in dislocation density and strain hardening magnitude under high strain-rate conditions remain to be fully determined; the precise strain-rate threshold at which dislocation multiplication becomes dominant over other deformation mechanisms is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi alloys with similar microstructural states. Subject specimens from both alloys to controlled high strain-rate tests simulating ballistic impacts. After testing, perform detailed TEM analysis to quantify dislocation density, and record stress–strain curves to derive strain hardening rates.
measurements: Dislocation density via TEM or in situ diffraction
Stress–strain curves to evaluate strain hardening rates
Comparative microstructural analysis pre- and post-deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under high strain-rate conditions the Mn-free alloy does not exhibit a significantly higher dislocation density and increased strain hardening relative to the Mn-containing alloy, then the hypothesis that dynamic mechanical performance is predominantly driven by dislocation multiplication (modulated by atomic bonding strength) is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising to provide effective antiballistic capability because of their superior mechanical properties. However, the twinning-active Cantor alloy is found less ballistic resistant, compared with its Mn-free companion. It is unclear how the HEAs resist ballistic impact and why Mn does not benefit the ballistic resistance. Here, we used molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the ballistic resistances of CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi and elucidate underlying mechanisms. It is shown that the alloys’ ballistic resistances dominantly benefit from active dislocations generated at higher strain rates. Stronger atomic bonding and higher dislocation densities make the CrFeCoNi easier to be strain hardened with elevated toughness to resist high-speed deformation, while weaker atomic bonding and easier occurrence of dislocation tangling make CrMnFeCoNi less resistant to failure under ballistic impact. This work helps better understand the antiballistic behavior of HEAs and guide the design of armor and energy-absorption materials. Cantor alloy’s fracture toughness exceeds 200 MPa·m1/2 at both cryogenic and room temperatures, which is exceptionally superior to those of conventional alloys. The fracture strain of Cantor alloy is strongly affected by the strain rate within the range 10−3 to 10 s−1 at high temperatures (), while its yield strength is insensitive to the strain rate at different temperatures (, ). Low temperature is found beneficial to the strain hardening of CrMnFeCoNi (), and annealing-induced abnormal hardening is observed after cold work, which is attributed to the long-range ordered structure ().
Because of their superior mechanical properties, especially the excellent strain hardening ability, the HEAs have great potential to be used for ballistic protection. However, there are very limited reports regarding the application or potential application of HEAs in ballistic protection ().
